utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Komljenovic. I hope you had a restful weekend.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Yes. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Komljenovic.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Since I have not been given the amount of time that I had asked for, I shall make an effort to ask questions that will be as clear as possible so that we can have them answered by a simple yes or no as often as possible, but, of course, you can always say more than that if you feel it is necessary. This is what I'd like to ask you: The critical event at Koricanske Stijene, was it motivated by a desire appropriate property although in such an abominable way? Was theft an important motive?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That certainly was one of the motives. We had received information that the persons who were killed had been robbed before that, and also we realised that in a restaurant called Zeka's, near Knezevo, they showed their booty, that is to say, the money and the jewellery they had stolen from these people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm waiting for the interpretation, and I'd like to ask you to -- ask for you to bear that in mind as well so that we do not have our words overlapping. You testified in the Ivankovic et al. case in the court of Bosnia-Herzegovina; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I'd like to remind you, 65 ter 22145, on page 14 -- or, rather, 72 in the document itself, you said that -- actually, the question was: "As a young, educated person, were you interested in whether you and the army and the CSB Banja Luka had acquired any knowledge, Prijedor, Knezevo, and so on and so forth? Were you interested in whether somebody had ordered that?" And you said: "I could not say yes. On the contrary. I had the impression that -- actually we don't have such material. On the contrary. We had the impression that people, the people I contacted, were more or less taken aback and surprised. More or less, as I said, and I had no assessment to the effect that somebody could have ordered this." Is that your position to this day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you said: "I tell you that this man had nothing to do with it. Zupljanin certainly didn't have anything to do with it. I know that Stojan Zupljanin would not have done that. He would not have ordered that, and I know that Stojan Zupljanin was shocked. Simo Drljaca - how do I put this? - had a different frame of mind, but I don't think that it was Simo either. In all likelihood Simo hadn't ordered this or approved of this. It was quite simply these young men, and the motive was primarily theft, and that is what I put to you." Is this your position to this day?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And then you had your first meeting in Banja Luka, in Mr. Zupljanin's office, and you noticed there that Mr. Zupljanin had taken a professional position that things had to be done in accordance with the law and that nothing should be hushed up, and you repeated that in your statement to the OTP. The 7th of December, 2009, page 5, 22144 is the page reference -- actually 65 ter reference and the page number is 5. I'm going to read it out in English so that it's interpreted. "[In English] Three or four months ago Vlado Glamocic admitted to me the following story which I heard for the first time. The night of the massacre, Glamocic received an enraged telephone call from Radovan Karadzic demanding answers about the massacre and who was responsible for it. Glamocic had just returned from a business trip and had no idea about the massacre but promised to call Karadzic the next day with more details. However, he said he never had any further contact with Karadzic concerning this and Karadzic never called him back. I assume that he found out through other channels. When I heard this, I was angry that Karadzic was putting us in the same box as the people from Prijedor who committed this crime." [Interpretation] Do you agree that you could make phone calls to Europe and Europe could make phone calls to your area but you could not get in touch with the eastern area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps I don't understand what you're saying. This is what it was all about. Vlado had told me that you had called him, and he said that you were angry. He said that the president was angry, that he was shouting, asking what was going on over there, "What have you done?" And that hurt us. "Who killed these people? What have you done?" Words to that effect. He sought information. Vlado had no information about what had happened. He had just arrived. We were hurt, as I said, because you put us all in one basket without knowing what had happened. Quite simply, you opened fire at us and them and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I was imprecise. I did not mean you personally. This is what I meant. Could you phone Banja Luka and Zagreb and Europe from Knezevo? Was that easier than making a phone call to Pale, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Pale and this part of Republika Srpska, the western part of Herzegovina including Pale or, quite simply, Banja Luka, the Krajina region was usually cut off during that period of time so this communication was very often nonexistent at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm asking you this because I'd like to remind you of something. Do you remember that on the 22nd of August, in London, a conference started, a conference that lasted until the 28th of August? So already on the 20th or 21st of August I flew to London. I conducted certain activities there. You do recall that this conference existed. Vance and Owen took over the conference on Bosnia from Carrington and Cutileiro. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Glamocic had an impression that I was calling from some trip and you mentioned that somewhere?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He actually said to me that you had called somewhere from the outside. He did not know what this was all about. He knew actually that you were abroad, that you were not in the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Subotic appeared on the 29th or 30th of August? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for the dates, I cannot confirm them with any precision, but Subotic did come twice. Two or three times he did come.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I do apologise for this impression that obviously remained, that I put you all in the same basket, but I'm just asking whether you could have called, not you personally but everybody, whether you could make phone calls. Do you understand that I did not have any other information? Well, now, if I tell you that the conference went only until the 27th, that on the 28th of August I flew to Belgrade, on the 29th I arrived in Pale, and I immediately asked General Subotic to go to that area, does that sound plausible to you?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, since you were abroad, and if you arrived on the 29th, on the 30th we had this meeting in Banja Luka, the meeting that we discussed here and that we saw the minutes of here. So it was on the 30th that Subotic chaired the meeting in Banja Luka, that's for sure, and that's when things started getting resolved. The people of Prijedor were given the task of being involved in the task that they were supposed to carry out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So General Subotic appeared there on behalf of the president of the republic. He addressed the executive government, and he asked for a pathologist to be involved and the judiciary organs, et cetera; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, those were the conclusions of this meeting that had been chaired by Mr. Subotic as defence minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The army brought one of the survivors to you -- or, rather, to your municipality, right, and then this survivor was taken in and sent to the Paprikovac hospital in Banja Luka for treatment, medical treatment. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The information I had was that the man who had survived had actually spent the night in Knezevo. Our people had saved him, and then he was taken to the hospital in Banja Luka, and afterwards he most probably went abroad.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your statement to the OTP on page 5, 22144, that's the 65 ter number, it's your December 2009 statement, you mention that had meeting with Subotic. You mentioned that you took Subotic to that particular spot. As minister of defence he was in charge of civilian protection as well; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Civilian protection also fell within the remit of the Ministry of Defence. It was a department within the Ministry of Defence. So the minister in charge was Minister Subotic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So that was the basis. That was the reason, not because the army would have had anything to do with it but simply because he was in charge of civilian protection as well. That is the reason why you took him to the scene.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Minister Subotic was in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You repeated that in your statement to the Office of the Prosecutor of Bosnia and Herzegovina in the Ivankovic case of the 27th of March, 2008, on page 4. It is the same document, 21445. You say, after a brief meeting, all of us who were present together with Minister Bogdan Subotic went to the scene, to Koricanske Stijene. In relation to this meeting at Alumina, what I remember is that it was not attended by Commander Bosko Peulic. The reason why the meeting was held in Alumina was the fact that Bosko Peulic did not want to receive Minister Bogdan Peulic [as interpreted] in the command of the 22nd Brigade that was at the post office building. Minister Subotic said that he was astonished by what had been done.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. These relations between Minister Subotic and Peulic were not very good. Generally speaking, the relations between us, the civilian authorities and the military structures, especially when the commander was Peulic, were not very good. If you wish, I can tell you later about some of the aspects involved with regard to these problems, that is, but that was one the reasons, because Subotic had already had some experience with Peulic, namely, he had announced his visit and that the other person simply refused to see him or, rather, avoided to see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you remember in the autumn of 1992 that was the reason or pretext for General Subotic to resign as minister and to join my military office? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that case. I am familiar with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the same case, on page 10 and 68 in the document itself, that's the 65 ter number 22145, you confirmed that the conclusion of that meeting was that the people of Prijedor should be involved and that they should have these bodies transferred to a proper place in order to make it possible for pathologists, forensic experts to have access to carry out all the necessary legal procedures and have these persons buried; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. These are the conclusions. This is the essence of the conclusions that were reached at that meeting that was chaired by Minister Subotic on the 30th of August. I wish to avail myself of this opportunity, perhaps I won't have another opportunity later, I hope that this statement of mine are going to affect the summary that we discussed last time. I do apologise to the Honourable Trial Chamber, but last time I did not manage to react in respect of certain details that were recorded in my summary. This is what it's all about. In part of the summary --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, I can say with certainty that you can stay assured. The summary does not form part of your evidence at all. So your testimony, a transcript, has been admitted in its entirety, so there will be no conclusion at all in the future, rest assured.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Karadzic, page 7, line 14, it's a question in relation to commander Bosko Peulic. The sentence as it reads now is like the following: "The reason why the meeting was held in Alumina was the fact that Bosko Peulic did not want to receive Minister Bogdan Peulic in the 22nd Brigade that was at the post office meeting." I take it the latter Bogdan Peulic should read "Subotic." Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quoted Mr. Komljenovic and what he stated to the BH prosecutor. The reason was that Bosko Peulic would not receive Mr. Bogdan Subotic at the command of the 22nd Brigade which was located in the postal building in Knezevo and so on and so forth. Our commanders had this kind of dismissive position towards the civilian authorities and would not always recognise their position as such; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I already said that it was particularly a problem when Peulic was in command. I just wanted to finish a sentence I began when I answered your previous question concerning the conclusions. I didn't mention in the conclusions or in any of my statements that the terrain should be cleansed by planting explosives. I said that people were simply buried on the spot by putting dirt over their bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 12 of the same document, which is page 70, you were asked whether after you had visited the location there was an on-site investigation, and you mentioned Prosecutor Pantic. Your answer was this. I quote: "Yes. Of course I cannot discuss whether the prosecution or Mr. Pantic or the people from his centre did something without us knowing. They probably did. They were trying to do their job since they were complaining they were unable to. I do suppose they visited the location, although I don't know what they did. I have no such information." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Given the scope of their authority and the tasks they were to perform, they were under no obligation to report to me as the municipal president, and I believe they did what they had to do without us knowing. I do know that they had trouble accessing the field because of the lay of the land, and this was the basic problem throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I wanted to show another diary page in order for you to interpret.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is P32769, although I believe these are only the pages that the Prosecution sought to tender. Hence we will need a 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This is just to check, Ms. Sutherland. The parts which Mr. Karadzic asked the witness so far, are they reflected in the 92 ter statement already, or he raised something new? I didn't have time to check them all.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. Are you talking about the witness's notebook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, the questions he asked in relation to the OTP statement and Ivankovic's transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Karadzic hasn't been giving page references and I'm having great difficulty in finding the portions that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you didn't check whether it has been already reflected in the 92 ter statement yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes -- no. That's correct, Your Honour. But in relation to the notebook, it's 65 ter number 13299.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. The reason I raised this is that if it is already in the evidence, of course it is for you to emphasise some important part. If you are short of time you don't have to do that in the future. That's all --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- I wanted to tell you, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. Can I add that the questions that Mr. Karadzic has been putting to the witness that come from his -- the statement given to the Bosnian prosecutor aren't in the draft amalgamated witness statement -- sorry, aren't in the witness's signed amalgamated statement because that only comes from the ICTY statement and his testimony before the BiH state court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. He asked several questions with respect to OTP statement and Ivankovic transcript. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, the -- the -- the questions put to him about the conversation that Mr. Karadzic had with Glamocic is contained in paragraph 5 of the amalgamated signed statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have page 785. In the English it is 7803 -- no, no, 21 of 37 in the English version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Tomljenovic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Komljenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: If you remember the previous page, this one should refer to the same meeting; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go two pages back? 83, and then 84, and finally 85 in the Serbian version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is the beginning of the meeting on the 30th of August; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe this was tendered by the Prosecution. Could we go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it not say the same thing: CSB Banja Luka, identification, civilian protection activities, doctors --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, could you help us find the English page.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's on -- it's got page 20 of 37, Your Honour, at the bottom of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I don't know whether this page was tendered by the Prosecution, but does it not say the following: "Identification. Engage civilian protection. Doctors. One bus from Prijedor. Food and lodging." All this had to do with the extraction of the corpses; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Judge Maric is mentioned, a check-point as well.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now go to the next page. And I know positively that that one was not tendered. It is also the next page in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it not say: "Information on meeting and statement and its jurisdictions"? What does it say? It seems that the jurisdiction had been dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me a moment. Yes. This is what it says. It mentions clearing up of the division of authority between civilian and military authorities, although I am confused by the mention of Major Trivic. I don't recall him being included in these issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, maybe you meant to say that he ought to be contacted. It doesn't say he was present.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall he was present, and he's not on the list of those present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What does it say further down?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "To the municipal organs on --"

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does it say "problems"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we see the other side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we in the correct page in English, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: It reads -- it seems that you or someone else proposed mixed police patrols; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mixed police patrols, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. "More frequent contacts with the Military Prosecutor and Military Court"; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then it says: "Responsible municipal organs, it should be raised to a higher level." What else? In any case, these are the conclusions of the meeting. Identification is what we mentioned in the previous page, tasks to the municipal organs, as well as mixed patrols and more frequent contact with the military prosecutor and the judiciary and the responsible civilian authorities, that issue should be sent to a higher level. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I seek to tender these pages, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, the pages will be added to the existing Exhibit P3769.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You were put a question by the Prosecutor in 2009 about how it came about that Krejic was replaced and Drljaca could not be. You said that there was an agreement in place in the municipality regarding Krejic, and for Drljaca it was quite different. If we tried to remove him, it would have well resulted in an uprising in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had a meeting of the Municipal Assembly and Board given the fact that we were facing certain problems which were under the remit of civilian police, primarily the security of property and citizens. That was our main problem. In other words, we had people coming back from the front lines shooting, getting drunk, threatened people, looted, and the police was unable to deal with it. On the other hand, they also had to participate in combat at the front line, the police, that is. We had a split of sorts. Some of us believed that the police should be in the civilian areas to protect the security of people and property, and we asked Chief Zupljanin to replace Krejic, but before that we had agreed with Krejic that he would be transferred to Banja Luka. It wasn't a problem in itself. With Drljaca the situation was quite different. He was quite a powerful man, and if Zupljanin had tried to replace him, he would have had to face a significant reaction on the part of authorities in Prijepolje and the area. In other words, I'm quite certain that Mr. Zupljanin was waiting for a more favourable moment to do something in order to have Drljaca removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krejic was replaced because you needed someone more decisive. Other than that, he had no faults.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. We simply wanted the police to take more -- a more active role in providing security for property and citizens and to go to the front lines less.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The position of the local authorities in Knezevo was that the entire incident should be investigated and that the perpetrators be prosecuted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, was your position identical to that of Mr. Zupljanin and Minister Subotic as well as that of my position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All the people I had been in contact at the time, all those who were in charge and who had to deal with the incident were shocked. They all insisted on keeping things within the law and that the bodies be extracted, identified, and the perpetrators prosecuted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The location of this tragic crime was very difficult to access; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It is next to the Ilomska River. It is a very deep canyon, and the crime took place in the location where the cliffs are particularly steep. It was indeed a great problem for those who were supposed to recover the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the Ivankovic et al. case, this is the same document, 65 ter 22145, page 9 and 10, in the document itself these are pages 67 and 68, there you described that your people tried to recover the bodies in order to hand them over to the pathologist and inspectors who were to take things up from there, but that it was a difficult thing to do. The people you had at your disposal were for the most part elderly and handicapped, who were not sent to the front line but, rather, they were part of the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We had mobilised a unit of the civilian protection before the meeting in Prijedor. Our great problem was that the Prijedor people refused or did not want to participate in the recovery of the bodies. The army took the same approach. They simply did not want to assist, and it was for that reason that we mobilised the civilian protection. However, it comprised mainly the elderly and people who were military unfit, and they had very poor equipment. They did try to recover some bodies, and they managed to recover four. They buried them initially next to the road, and later on other investigative measures were taken concerning those bodies. But that was the extent of what our civilian protection could do at the time. Time went by and we simply could not wait any longer. It was next to the river, and the weather was quite warm, and given the fact that everyone else refused to help, we from that area wanted to approach it in a humane way, to deal with it properly, since those who could assist refused. I wanted to say another thing because I don't know if I'll have an opportunity later. Concerning this task, much as other tasks in the civilian sphere was approached in the very same way, although this was not in the territory of the Knezevo municipality, we still addressed the issue. The law on the annexation of our municipality to the Vlasic municipality was proclaimed on the 17th of December, 1992, and it began being implemented on the 30th of December, 1992. It was in the war area and was not legally under the jurisdiction of the municipality or perhaps not even in the RS necessarily. We had tried to assist the civilians in the area, because they were unable to access their home municipality of Travnik, and we assisted in the civilian sphere. In other words, we organised the work of the school, provided utilities, food, and then the incident took place. We simply could not remain uninvolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: There is something missing in the transcript. Actually it says that the republic was not in charge but it's actually the military.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that it was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska and that this was a war zone, a grey zone, but from a formal legal point of view, since we had not had a law, the law was passed later. As regards civilian activities, this was an area that nobody was in charge of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your testimony in Ivankovic, on page 72 in the document itself, you say that as far as you know, the brigade got involved partly in terms of securing the scene but that they did not do anything else. Is that along the lines of what you've been saying, namely that no one really wanted to get involved because everybody was horrified by what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Everybody avoided getting involved, especially the brigade commander. As a matter of fact, we asked him to give us men and equipment so that we tried to get the victims out. However, since the army had not been involved in this directly, he did not want to meddle, as you had said, and we stayed at the public security centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Ivankovic case, on page 96 in this document, otherwise it is page 38 of this testimony, you were asked about your links with the headquarters, the president of the Municipal Assembly, the government, the ministers and so on, and you said there that you did not inform anyone, that you did not send any reports. You also said that there were no headquarters, basically. "We were duty-bound to write reports to the Assembly, government, president, republic. That was not the usual form of communication." The Defence attorney says: "So, written reports?" Answer, you say: "In that year, 1992, I know -- and I'm not sure what the telephone lines were like. I know that to Banja Luka we did have links but from Banja Luka very difficult, very difficult in this case. The centre of public security was a regional centre and that was it basically." Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle that's it. That year we were more or less left to our own resources. The contacts we had with the government and certain ministers were like this: You sort of have a problem, and then you tried to get a hold of someone in this way or that way or through somebody else in order to have things resolved. As for communication -- as for communication with the government, I mean in terms of formal communication, practically there was none. We never wrote any reports. We never gave any explanations. Quite simply, that was not the communication that was there. There was practically no communication. Also telephones were down and various other links. We in the Krajina were totally isolated at the time, generally speaking. It was hard for us to get supplies. In Banja Luka, 12 babies died that summer because there was no oxygen, and nobody got worried about that. Twelve new-born babies died in July in Banja Luka, and nobody did a thing about it, humanitarian organisations, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So you established this school in part of the territory of the municipality of Travnik without any government assistance. It was the municipality that did that; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We sent a teacher there. The school had already existed. We just didn't want the children to be out of school. There were very few children there, though, so we did that on our own. Also that summer we worked on a transmission line so that they would have electricity out there, although we did not have electricity all the time either. Then we organised medicare there. We had a doctor who went there once a week from Knezevo. That's the kind of work we did on our own, if I can put it that way again, because we felt duty-bound towards the civilian population. The law was passed only later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As for these communication problems, you spoke about that here on page 2 and 3, 22144 is the 65 ter number of the document. So that's what you said to the OTP here as well, namely that the SDS had a statute and programme and that in principle this was being implemented. However, in 1992, there was no communication between the ARK Krajina and the centre in Pale. Also in that period you did not submit any written reports to the Main Board of the SDS; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: "Reports" instead of "properties." [Interpretation] I did not submit any written reports. The transcript says "properties" and the word used was "reports." Line 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: From this point of view, did all of the Krajina feel isolated, and did they have to function independently from Sarajevo -- rather, Pale? Did they have to make do and make decisions on their own throughout 1992, at least?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The Krajina was compelled to act that way. We had already established the Autonomous Region of the Krajina as an economic region. Absolutely motivated by economic motives. The institute in Banja Luka had conducted certain analyses and worked out certain parameters and came to the conclusion that Banja Luka was seriously lagging behind Sarajevo, that money was flowing out of Banja Luka and very little was being returned, and therefore something had to be done. So a region was established, an autonomous region, to provide for proper economic development. That was our line of thinking at the time. It was a multi-ethnic region. When the war started in 1992, things took a different turn, of course, the way we didn't really want them to develop. The entire area of Banja Luka was completely cut off from the rest of Republika Srpska, and we were compelled to have a type of state organisation in order to survive, because we did not have any contacts with headquarters, and we did not know how things would develop. That was one side of the problem. And then there was this other problem, namely, that there was this danger of going into total separatism. There was always this relationship between Pale and Banja Luka. Banja Luka wanted to be independent and to run itself, and then there's Pale. In view of the mentality involved and the kind of people we are, Pale was worried that this might go too far.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the OTP -- in your statement to the OTP, 22144, on page 3, you mention that Skender Vakuf joined the community of municipality of Bosanska Krajina on the 12th of April, 1991. It's a good thing that you brought this up. 1D4453. Let's have a look at that. 1D4453. That is the transcript of the founding Assembly of the community of municipalities of Bosanska Krajina. Was your position the following: That you had not received any instructions from the top echelons of government or of the party?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for this enterprise, as you called it, we carried this out out of fear for our own future. We were aware of the Krajina being the Krajina and that very easily we could be left out on our own, and that is what ultimately happened. The director of the institute, Professor Jaksic, also attended this meeting, and he presented an analysis to us of how much Banja Luka and the region were lagging behind economically. So this was our decision which was primarily motivated by economic reasons. However, this was not the only decision of ours that was not being co-ordinated with Pale, although -- although these misunderstandings, these sparks between Banja Luka and Pale existed throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would not say Banja Luka and Pale only, but Banja Luka and Pale, there was this kind of rivalry, primarily because of the money that was flowing out. I would also like to refer to another decision that was not in accord with your policy, and I can say that for sure, at least not the policy that you pursued at the time and also the official Belgrade. That is to say, this decision made in Grahovo to join the Krajina in 1991. That is when we all -- that is when we were all attacked, rather, by this decision that we had taken on our own. I remember some details from that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland. I remember you rose.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It doesn't matter, Your Honour. I was just wanting to have the correct document on the screen. We're talking about April 1991, and it appears that there's a document on the screen 17th of November, 1992, and I just wanted the correct Defence 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. 1D4451, 4451. Let's see this decision on accession. I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: While we're waiting for that, Mr. Komljenovic, do we agree that this rash and wilful step taken by the two Krajinas was based on the fear of the Serbs in Croatia that they would suffer greatly and face great difficulties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Unfortunately, after the elections and after the victory of the HDZ, and after the HDZ announced its policy and especially when the HDZ moved from rhetoric to actual implementation of this policy, especially after the constitution of the Republic of Croatia and when the Serbs lost their status as a constituent people, they realised that they would face a great deal of difficulty in Croatia. This was also based on history. The suffering of the Serbs in Croatia is a well-known fact. So this was a justified fear. It proved to be true. That is one thing. On the other hand, we in Krajina were afraid that we would be cut off from the rest of the republic and Serbia. So there was fear on both sides, and that is why we organised ourselves politically in order to survive quite simply.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid this is not that either. 1D4451 is the document that I asked for.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That should be the decision of your municipality on acceding to or, rather, joining -- well, actually, were you part of a community of municipalities before that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was some community of municipalities. Skender Vakuf earlier on belonged to the Krajina. So there was some structure that existed even during the days of Communism, the previous government. So basically we did not change our status. We stayed where we had been. However, we confirmed this organisation. First of all, we established this community of municipalities and then an autonomous region. We were the only ones in BH who created a region rather than a district, an SAO, as others did. So we really built up this region. Those were our motives, a multi-ethnic region for purely economic reasons. Later on, it proved to be necessary to have a political organisation as well, that is to say, to create a state or certain state structures, as it were, because we were isolated. We were on our own. That was this latent and constant fear that prevailed in the Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You must be referring to 1D4551 and not 4451.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right, Your Excellency. I have the wrong number. We've just noticed that. 1D4551. Could we have that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is that decision of yours, the one that you signed, the decision of the Municipal Assembly. You were part of the community of municipalities of Banja Luka, but now it was called the Bosnian Krajina Association of Municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can this be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1889, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like to ask that we go through some parts of the transcript of this founding Assembly. 1D4453. It's probably 4553. There was another bit of confusion. Yes. This is the transcript. We probably have it in English as well. Thank you. Page 3, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in the box we have Kovacevic's contribution. He greeted all these present, and we have a reference to HDZ representatives being present who became members of the Assembly as well as of the SDA and the SDS. Can we go to the next page. Does he not mention the three parties?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they became members of the newly founded Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page in English as well. Before Dusko Jaksic speaks, Kovacevic says that he would also like to greet Dusko Jaksic, director of the economic institute, who explained the economic reasons why a decentralisation is necessary, in other words, to have a more independent Bosnian Krajina which would be free of -- of the influence of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since this is a matter of economics, I will not go into details, but could we have it admitted nonetheless? Could we go to page 10 -- sorry 12. 1230. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: We have Mr. Brdjanin speaking. He greeted everyone, and then he says the following: "Since we are trying to organise economic and cultural autonomy, we will also as a region ask that the fate of our region be kept within Bosnia and that Bosnia remain part of Yugoslavia." Was that so in April of 1991? Was it an acceptable position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was the official position of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: The next page, please. Here he says: "It seems that we relied too much on our heroic images and this was used by others who left us in the margins. We only want Mr. Izetbegovic, our president, to change his position. He wants a loose federation, and we want an independent Bosnia-Herzegovina. We refuse any kind of centralism or concentration of capital and power in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Finally, I am personally convinced that regionalisation would assist the stability of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Why? Because all three peoples reside in the area, as well as other ethnicities. By doing so, we would reduce ethnic tensions, and I believe any Muslim, Serb, or Croat would care more for the development of Banja Luka if they are Banja Luka residents rather than have Mostar do the same." Do you recall his words?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Brdjanin, in other words, supported Jaksic's position and the arguments from his analysis.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the entire region backed his analysis, and it was based on that study of the institute we implemented certain decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we go to the next page. We see here that 21 municipalities were represented but that only 14 municipalities voted today. The 15th was on the way. Fourteen municipalities, in other words, joined the project, whereas 21 were present in total, and the remainder of the municipalities simply awaited to see what the income -- what the outcome would be. Thank you. Can we now look at page 22, please. Here Mr. Vukic as the president of the Regional Board of the SDS advocates that people shouldn't be talking on behalf of the parties, but, rather, on behalf of the people, that different opinions should also be heard, and it says that the project of economic reorganisation has started. At the very bottom of the page -- [In English] Just a moment. Two pages -- at least one page more. Another, please. [Interpretation] Yes. Here Vukic says that the economic regionalisation race has begun, and then at the bottom, line 27 in Serbian, Josip Juric from Mrkonjic Grad, HDZ president in Mrkonjic Grad, also spoke; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And now can we go to the following pages both in Serbian and in English. Here Juric says that he had come to find out for himself the justification, the economic justification of the gathering and this regionalisation. Mrkonjic Grad has sustained from giving a statement and giving support to this gathering but wasn't against it because that would mean it was against the economic justification of this unification. Further on he says, at the bottom: "If we want this economic organisation of the community of Banja Luka municipalities, it must primarily be done at the economic level, and I tell you that the Mrkonjic Grad HDZ will vote for this organisation," and so on and so forth. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 25 and the corresponding page in English. Twenty-five in Serbian. Here Nedeljko Rasula, the president of the municipality of Sanski Most, speaks, and he says that, "If the figures don't mean anything, I don't know what should be the argument for a common strive to live in better conditions," and so on and so forth. He says that there would be less austerity, there would be less talk of who's Serb, who's Muslim, who's Croat, and he further on supports the elaborate presented [as interpreted] by Mr. Jaksic; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to the following page both in Serbian and in English. He ends by saying, "Let's try and trust each other, and if we don't trust each other's words, then we have to trust statistics." And then you say that you're from Skender Vakuf and that Skender Vakuf is one of the least developed municipalities in Bosnia and Herzegovina. And further on you say, "The municipality that we set up, we called it Bosnian municipality." Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We were obviously dissatisfied with our position. The fact was that we were the least developed municipality in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that supported thesis that was presented by Professor Jaksic, and that was that the whole of Krajina was largely underdeveloped and lagging behind the rest of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now go to page 33. It is the secretary, Dusko Djajic, who speaks here and says that the association is regulated by the constitutional amendment 42. This is a constitutional and legal matter, and it says that the municipalities that are linked territorially and economically do so in order to exercise their rights, and on that condition they can associate into a -- an association of municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He referred to the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina and its amendment 42. We wanted to development an economic region.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and the accused please be asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is secretary Dusko Djajic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you are being asked to slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best. However, I'm under the pressure of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In your answer, you say -- you said "constitution" but that was not recorded properly. He said that he was referring to the constitution; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina, amendment 42.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This has to be corrected on line 16. Please bear with me. I have to skip pages. There was reference to the elections. I am going to skip.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That was a vote of confidence which was secret?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was a secret vote. We had three or four candidates. We voted. Municipal Assemblies delegated their delegates to represent them in the association of municipalities of Bosnian Krajina, and they elected a president. I believe that we had three or four candidates including Brdjanin, Kupresanin, a gentleman for Drvar called Knezevic, and I don't know if there was a fourth candidate. The Assembly was set up based on the free electoral will and local Assemblies were set up after the elections in 1992 -- one, and then the municipalities delegated candidates for the association of municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they had the electoral legitimatity [as interpreted]?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was derived from the elections.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can we now go to page 52 in Serbian. Here Mr. Kupresanin thanks the Serbs, the Muslims and Croatians for having placed trust in him, and he congratulates people for having established the Assembly of Krajina. Can we go to the fall -- following page. English could be 53 or 54. It should be a lower number. One before. Here Mr. Kupresanin expresses his gratitude, and he says that there will be no borders, that our name is Bosnian Krajina, not Krajina. We are not breaking up the borders of Bosnia. Everybody should know that. And we also say that the time for democracy has come, and according to amendment 42, in keeping with the federal and republican laws we have set up a region and nobody can tell us that we are in breach of any laws. And further on he says, we people from Krajina have a lot of tasks in front of us. We are going to carry out a lot of reforms in education, health care, and so on and of -- we are going to develop an affluent village, and we will not support the republican federation. Was that all that based on economic premise and logic; and do you remember that of the 100 dinars that went from Krajina to Sarajevo only 18 dinars returned to the municipalities in Krajina?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that was the main problem, the principal problem, and Professor Jaksic, as the director of the institute, in his speech that lasted two or three hours provided certain indicators that spoke about Banja Luka which contributed to the budget of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In view of how much Krajina and Banja Luka gave to the budget of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Banja Luka is at a huge loss because there was an outpour of the money into Sarajevo, and that Sarajevo was developing at the expense of the region and at the expense of Banja Luka. That was the main matrix of the meeting and of the policies that were adopted, and the decision was based on an analysis of that kind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't see that any one of us from the headquarters of SDS or the government on the Serbian side either spoke or were present?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the whole document be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Any objections, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Just one moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have any objection to the pages that were discussed with the witness being tendered -- being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So you'd suggest not admitting those pages not shown to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The problem is identifying those pages. So if the Defence, in co-operation with the Prosecution, identify to the Registry later on those page numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And also, Your Honour, perhaps the Defence might like to give it a better description than transcript of AV00-4354 and a date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That means there exists a video/audio-clip for this Assembly, but what they are admitting is only the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, but it would be preferable to have a proper description in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be done with the co-operation from the Defence. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D1890, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to explain to all of us what were the views of Skender Vakuf municipalities -- municipality of the needs of Croats and Muslims? I have a list of settlements here, and I can see that as far as Muslims were concerned, in the villages there were either 0 or 2 or 3 Muslims in Zivinice. There were 2 Muslims, for example, in Dobratic. There were 3 Muslims, and 3 Serbs, and the rest were Croats. Is it correct that few villages in Skender Vakuf were more or less uniform in terms of ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In Skender Vakuf Muslims -- 95 per cent of Muslims lived in the centre of Skender Vakuf. There were about 5.000 of them altogether. There were only about a dozen houses in a little village. Serbs were more or less homogeneous in the villages, and Croats were also homogenous, and they resided in -- resided in a neighbourhood that we called Pogari, on the left bank of the Ugar River, and also they lived in Ugartici [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In geographic terms they were separated from you by the canyon. It would have been more normal for them to belong to Jajce?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. They followed an economic logic as well, the same kind of logic that we've governed when we set up our region. Primarily the roads were better towards Jajce. Jajce was a more developed municipality than Skender Vakuf, and they were also dissatisfied with their own status, their own economic status. The -- our area was underdeveloped, and they wanted to leave Skender Vakuf for those reasons. They wanted to develop faster, and they wanted to be tied to Jajce. In Jajce there was already the will and infrastructure in place. They submitted a request to be joined to Jajce. We issued a decision consenting to their request. We were in favour of them changing their municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have also answered my next question, and that was about your reaction, i.e., you respected that. You were in favour of them either setting up their own municipality or joining Jajce?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We fully understood their position. Their position was absolutely clear to us. They had every reason to be dissatisfied with their status, primarily with their economic status, and they sought ways to deal with that problem in a more adequate way. We spoke with representatives of Croats. Later on we had very correct relations with them. I don't know whether I should remind everybody of some of our agreements. Based on your suggestions and agreements with Boban, in 1992 we had an agreement with the Croats according to which all the local issues should be dealt with peacefully without embarking on any conflicts. And in that sense we had meetings with the representatives of HDZ from Central Bosnia and Travnik, with the president of the Executive Board of Travnik Mr. Boris Matisic. And with your leave, I would like to share an event with you just to illustrate how things were at the time. Since we were aware of your agreement with Boban according to which we were to avoid any conflicts wherever possible, and there was an attempt for the local communes to get in touch with each other in order to further that initiative on the peaceful solution to the problems in Bosnia-Herzegovina from the grassroots, as it were, we were one of the municipalities that accepted that initiative, and together with the representatives of the Croatian people we agreed that we would not embark on any conflicts. On one occasion, the war had already started, I spent some time in Travnik. I visited President Boris Matisic. It was on the occasion of their Catholic Christmas. I paid them a visit. In return he promised to visit us and to celebrate our -- the Catholic Easter in spring 1992, and he was supposed to visit me on Mount Vlasic for our Orthodox Easter. We were well received in Travnik and we confirmed our will not to enter into conflicts. However, on the day when he was supposed to pay me a visit he was arrested and taken to the military police command. Actually, that is a problem which illustrates very well how we functioned. In military circles, in some military circles there was a need for those peaceful -- peace initiatives, albeit at the local level, to be thwarted and prevented. We were taken by surprise as people -- because we had invited the man and they arrested him. We wanted to save our own dignity. We tried to save him, and we managed to take him out of the prison owing to another colonel who was the chief of security in -- in -- in Banja Luka Corps, the late Colonel Milan Stevilovic. At our request he understood our situation and need to preserve peace and preserve contacts with the people who were very fair to us so he set that man free, and that night, Mr. Matisic and another officer of the HVO were returned to Travnik in our vehicles. And that's how we saved him and we also saved our face. Unfortunately, certain military circles did not respect us and they created a lot of confusion in order to disturb the relationships that we had been building.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Just one last question before the break. Is it correct that this careful relationship you had with your Croat neighbours resulted in tens of thousands of civilians being received in Vlasic as well as HVO soldiers? They had been driven out of Travnik by the Muslim forces. You provided accommodation for them there and then let them go to what -- wherever they wanted. You provided some assistance in terms of food as well.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but there was another event that I wanted to mention which followed Matisic's arrest and his release. Four soldiers of ours found themselves at an HVO check-point by mistake and then they were taken prisoner. I believe they were still JNA soldiers because the JNA was still in the area. There were young soldiers accompanied by a lieutenant. Mr. Matisic did as we expected he would. He returned them the very next day and our cooperation continued. The event you refer to took place in the spring of 1993, when Muslim forces launched a large offensive on Croat positions in the Lasva Valley in Central Bosnia. During that time, our army was at Vlasic, and as regards our units, they did not take part in any combat. At that point in time, we managed to save between 2 and 3.000 HVO members, women and children who had fled in front of advancing Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I'm looking at the clock, Your Excellency. Is it a good time for a break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll have a -- yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, just before we break in relation to that last document, I was under the misguided impression it was around 150 pages, and given that it is a third of that and the number of pages that were read out by the accused, I think it may be easier to admit the document in its entirety.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I tend to agree with you. That document will be admitted in its entirety. Yes. We'll take a break for half an hour and resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, I wanted to ask for your indulgence and ask for some additional time for this witness since I have a number of topics left which I plan to cover quickly, but I truly need his presence here to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What amount of time do you have in mind when you ask for extension, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at least another half an hour to the one I have. I didn't want to ask for an entire session of 90 minutes, but if I were to receive an additional 30 minutes, I believe I could complete it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber will allow your request, Mr. Karadzic, but that does not mean that you can ask any questions. Just please focus, be focused, and concentrate on relevant and important issues, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellencies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, in 2009, you were asked by the Prosecution about something you discussed with my team as well. It's a matter of Variants 1 and B -- A and B. In paragraph 12, which is 65 ter 22144 on page 3, you said that you did not remember having attended a December meeting when the instructions were handed out, and you added that it did not concern your municipality of Skender Vakuf. Is it correct that you heard of the document containing the Variants A and B only after the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that you did not undertake any measures in your municipality based on that piece of paper?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never received it, and naturally we didn't follow it through. We didn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Is it correct that Jovan Cizmovic did not get in touch with you with regard to that document?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mr. Cizmovic only as a prominent lawyer from Banja Luka. As regards his engagement at the time, I know he belonged to another political party. Concerning this specific issue, we had no contact with Cizmovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As an SDS official and municipal president, do you agree you would have had to receive -- receive that document if it was binding on all party members?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is -- if the president of the party and the bodies of the party were issuing instructions to the lower level, that is to say Municipal Boards, it would have been logical that all Municipal Boards had received it. In such circumstances, I would expect to have received it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In 2009, on page 3 of the 65 ter 22144, you discussed the matter of arming. I will read out that portion, although it's probably part of some transcript. "[In English] We had discussed arming the Serbs because the SDA in Mahala were accusing us of this. There were rumours that the Muslims were going to take over things like the power plant, waterworks, et cetera. These rumours created a great deal of fear. Everyone wanted weapons on all sides and everyone wanted to be armed. I cannot confirm nor deny that the army provided other Serbs with weapons during this time, but I did not have anything to do with that." [Interpretation] Was it indeed so, and has anything changed in the meantime in your position?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's nothing to change. There was a problem immediately prior to the war which was that fear was spreading. It's a different thing whether it was based on any real terms or not. However, in Knezevo, there were rumours that Croats and Muslims were arming themselves. By the same token, the Muslims on the other side probably discussed Serbs arming themselves. It all increased tensions, and we were afraid that the Muslims in Skender Vakuf, if given weapons, could occupy key infrastructure in the municipality such as the pipelines, the electricity grid, and some other facilities. We were in direct contact with our Muslim citizens, and we were aware of their fear too. I would use an illustration here. They made a request, which I believe may clarify another important dimension. It had to do with the convoys which went through Knezevo. On a certain day, our Muslim -- or, rather, Bosniak residents and their representatives came to see me. They wanted to leave the municipality as they were afraid, and I feel free to say that they were justified in feeling that way. They asked for guarantees for their safety, for the safety of their lives and property. They asked that a decision be made by the municipal organs. We found ourselves in dire straits. If we were to make a decision, a consequence of that could be that they would interpret it as our wish for them to leave. If we failed to act, we were then concerned about their safety. They asked for guarantees that things would be fine, and we, on the other hand, given that we had no armed force at our disposal, neither military nor police, could not provide such guarantees. In case of an incident, we believed that it could prove to be a great mistake. That is why we were afraid for their fate, and we told them that if they really wanted to leave that they should leave alone, by themselves. The situation at the time was that the three ethnic communities simply moved from one territory to another. In the summer of 1992 [as interpreted], those who had initially been driven out of Croatia arrived in Knezevo. They came to Slavonia, towns such as Bakrac, Lipik and Pozega. It was on the eve of the war in Croatia or at the very beginning of that conflict. The people in question were our citizens who had emigrated to Croatia in the 1970s and '80s. The next wave arrived from Central Bosnia, from the Lasva Valley and Travnik, as well as Novi Travnik. Serbs used auxiliary side roads, often through forests, and many never arrived to their destinations. By the same token, members of the Croat or Muslim communities who tried to flee frequently went to stay with their families and relatives. In other words, people were trying to save their lives. For the reasons of their safety, some municipalities decided to organise such convoys while others did not. We did try to convince our neighbours to stay, but we were in no position to provide the guarantees we were supposed to. We were afraid that a lunatic such as the people who were at Koricani could create such an incident, and then we would find ourselves in a very grave situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is the second time the witness has given a rather long answer, over a page of transcript, to a question that simply had to do with the arming of -- the arming of the population. So I would ask if Mr. Karadzic can control his witness -- the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, it is for the witness. But if you give simpler answers, then the accused would be more benefitted. Please bear that in mind, Mr. Komljenovic. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. An intervention in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You said that the first wave of refugees arrived in 1991, during the clashes in Croatia, whereas we have the summer of 1992 in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first refugees who arrived in the then Skender Vakuf arrived in the fall of 1991. That's when the first wave of mobilisation took place by the JNA and the war in Croatia began. So the initial refugees received in Knezevo were there in the fall of 1991.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Those refugees from Croatia and Central Bosnia, did they present a burden, economically speaking, for you and were you -- were you not afraid that their anger would turn against domestic Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was a great burden for the community given the fact that it was at the beginning of the war and that there were no organised structures who could provide humanitarian assistance. Some assistance came through the Red Cross while we provided a lot of it ourselves. It was a problem in its own right. As for the other part of your question, it was clear that such a thing -- such an emotion could spill over. The people who arrived in Knezevo were frustrated by the fact that they had been expelled, and always potentially at risk of creating a disturbance in Knezevo itself [Realtime transcript read in error "it testified"].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In addition to the problem with those who had been expelled, is it not correct that you did not have any local paramilitary groups, but you had other groups passing through your area such as the White Eagles, and you had people coming back from the front lines at rotations? Were there incidents where they would freely enter shops and take alcohol and that your -- that both Serb and Muslim citizens felt in danger?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were to ask the Serbs or Croats or Muslims in Knezevo, we probably would not have ever had war. The problem was the people who transited through Knezevo. They disturbed all of our residents. There were cases of robberies, shootings, and other disturbances. It was all created by those who simply went through Knezevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Line 21, it says "it testified." That is an extra. It doesn't belong there. Still, you had no murder incidents. We had a policeman of yours here who said that there were a few murders before the war and a couple during the war, and these were isolated incidents involving a very limited number of people.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. If we look at what was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina in general and the war, with its toll, and although Knezevo was not an isolated island, we were very happy with the situation in our municipality since there were very few things happening. I think all in all there were five murders because of different motives, but they were all processed by our public security station in keeping with the law. It is something that the whole of Knezevo can be proud of. Of course, there was the Koricanske Stijene incident which had a certain impact, but we still believe that it was outside the territory of our municipality, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Was it also important that the municipality of Knezevo is between Kotor Varos and Jajce and immediately adjacent to you was Siprage with a large number of Muslims residing there?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knezevo indeed was between the territories you mentioned. There was Ugar where Croats and Muslims were, and on the other side there were Siprage and Vecici which were Muslim strongholds. We were simply wedged into that part.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. SDA president Suljo Susic --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Susic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: He came to see you with a delegation asking for their organised departure. Did they indeed leave of their own accord, and did many of them leave Kotor Varos -- sorry, Skender Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Knezevo or Skender Vakuf. Since we could not grant their request and since we could not guarantee their safety, as I've explained, they left of their own accord. They took whatever vehicles and movable property they had, and without our knowledge, in a matter of a couple of days, they simply left. At that point in time we saw it as their salvation because we couldn't provide what they wanted. Many of them left their property behind, and they left the keys to their real estate, to their acquaintances and relatives. In that regard there were no specific incidences. After the war they all returned, and for the most part their property had been preserved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. A lot of people returned, therefore, and their property was returned. Even those who didn't return could get their property back.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Everybody got their property back. I would like to re-emphasise that all of the property save for a few sporadic cases, all the poverty was saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up 1D4552.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, although it may have not reached you in time due to interrupted communications, that the government had put a ban on the sale of property? It had put a ban on the sale of apartments. And during the war things like that were scrutinised. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: This is from the 188th session of the Executive Board of the government in Banja Luka. It was held in November 1994. I'm interested in page 3. While we're waiting for the page to appear, Mr. Komljenovic, let me ask you to explain in the shortest possible term for the benefit of all the participants in the trial the term of "social assets." This is something that doesn't exist in their countries when we're talking about apartments and other non-private property.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This socially owned property is a phenomenon typical of the former Yugoslavia. It was a dominant type of property during the entire rule of the Communist League. There were no private companies. All of the companies were state companies to start with and later on socially owned companies.
