The apartments that were built in the former Yugoslavia were built with the allocations from the budget, around they were given to workers and officials to use, but those people were not their owners. They were just the users of those apartments. It was only later on, after the end of the war, new authorities will introduce a new law on privatisation, so the people who used the apartments were given the right to buy them at a much reduced price. So today they're the owners of those apartments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please look at paragraph 1 -- bullet point 1 where it says that consent is given to exchange municipal apartments. So the apartment provider and owner was the municipality?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The owner of the apartment had to be a municipality, a company or some state body.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We see that Semiz -- Amina Semiz, Amina Semiz, is she a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by the name I would assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Amina Semiz is hereby allowed to exchange her apartment with Stjepan Omicevic [phoen]. Stjepan could be a Serb or a Croat; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Although I suppose that he was probably a Croat. It is more likely that he was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now you can see what is approved by way of exchanging municipal apartments. Sometimes the protagonists are Muslims and Serbs, sometimes Croats as well. Goran Arnautovic is probably a Croat. And towards the end of the page, in conclusion we can see that a municipal apartments were assigned to people for use; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And then under bullet point 4, a decision was issued that you should also be assigned a municipal apartment in October 1994. Is that the time when you were transferred to Banja Luka?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we go to page 5 now. We can see here that Husein Bahtijarevic [phoen], obviously a Muslim, request was rejected - he wanted to exchange his apartment with Miroslav Kopanja from Zenica - because that exchange was fictitious. And further on, another request was rejected. The applicant was Kemal Bibuljica, also a Muslim, who wanted to exchange his municipal apartment with Milan Momic. Again the exchange would have been fictitious. So fictitious exchanges were not permitted.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what is meant by this term "fictitious." What does it mean when they say a fictitious exchange of an apartment? I'm not sure that I understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that the apartment doesn't exist at all or that there is not an exchange but a sale of an apartment?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably that would be the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then on the following page there is another example of the same kind and then on page 10 in the same document, page 10, the right is denied to Muslim, Croats, and Serbs to --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can we zoom in? Can we blow-up that part so I can read it? Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And here you agree with me, don't you, that there are Serbs, Croats, and Muslims here; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There's Matic, for example, Delibasic, Jokanovic. So I would say there were all kinds, Croats, Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit D1891, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, according to what you know, in your municipality or any municipality for that matter, those who were resettled because of fear, did it ever become possible for them not to come back?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with that. After the war, it was a common policy for everybody to come back. That was established in the Dayton Accord. This is one of the elementary human rights. I believe that we were aware of the fact that those people were only leaving temporarily to save themselves and, God willing, that they would be back. That was the only possible solution in all of our minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The health minister who was also dealing with humanitarian issues, Mr. Dragan Kalanic, on my behalf on the 22nd of May, 1992, signed a commitment to organise the resettlement of the population from war-struck areas and areas of combat -- combat activities. It says there that the municipality addressed by the population is duty-bound to provide a police escort and to inform all the municipalities through which they would pass as well as the municipality that would receive them, that they should all be ready to receive them. Do you agree that before that signature was put on the document there was no organised resettlement of the population under escort but that, rather, everybody was running into chaotic matter whenever -- wherever they could.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I can't tell you that I am aware of this decision by Mr. -- Minister Kalanic. At least we did not receive it. Although I spoke about that. I said that people were leaving in an organised or -- way or otherwise in order to save themselves and that some municipalities resorted to the organised manners, whereas the others couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You also mentioned that Serbs from Central Bosnia fled to the Republika Srpska across Vlasic using auxiliary roads in a chaotic manner. Was there a single organised convoy of Serbs under escort, or did they continue fleeing as best as they could until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Serbs fled in a haphazard way. There were also cases of exchanges on the line. I believe that the army occasionally organised those exchanges of civilians for civilians, soldiers for soldiers. And in such cases, I suppose that they would arrive in an organised manner. However, for the large part, Serbs left Central Bosnia in a chaotic way by running, fleeing, using auxiliary routes, making their way through to our municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask you something about the practice of work of Crisis Staffs, i.e., Councils for National Defence. In your testimony in the Ivankovic case, which is 65 ter 22145 on page 3, and in the document it's page 61, to the Prosecutor's question as to whether the Assembly of Knezevo was also a part of the Crisis Staff, you say that it depended on the stage of the war, and I quote: "In the first stage, on the eve of the war, and when the war just started we functioned as a council for national defence pursuant to the old law. I don't remember the name of the law. It was a federal law. Later on it depended on the course of developments. First they were -- remained as Crisis Staffs and then War Staffs." Can you please tell us something about that practice. As the president of the municipality, you were also the president of the Council of National Defence.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We inherited the organisational structure that was based on the federal Law on National Defence, according to which at the federal level there were Secretariats for National Defence and social self-protections, and similar organs existed at the republican level. Bosnia-Herzegovina had a body of that kind. It was a -- a Secretariat for National Defence and civilian protection and Territorial Defence. Local communes and municipalities had similar municipal organs and municipal secretariats that -- that had their secretaries and their small administrations. At that time, at the -- the beginning, mobilisation was organised by superior bodies. According to that law, in case of war or a -- or an imminent threat of war when local Municipal Assemblies could not be called up and couldn't function, the Council for National Council [as interpreted] would take over their duties. I was the president of the council of national defence, and in addition to myself there was the chief of the local police, the President of the Executive Board, the secretary of the Secretariat of National Defence, the commander of the Territorial Defence Staff. Those were members by virtue of their position who had also to be members of that council. I believe that those councils remained functioning throughout the entire 1992, but I'm not sure. However, at a certain stage they were renamed the -- in a certain way, although I did not see any such decision or instruction. They were then called Crisis Staffs. Towards the end of the war, they were renamed as War Staffs. I don't know why that was done, because in essence it didn't change anything. The same people remained members of the body, and their authorities and competencies remained the same. The -- the -- those authorities were civilian authorities more or less, and that remained the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On line 7 there is a mistake in the transcript. It should read Council for National Defence rather than Council for National Council. This is the federal Council for National Defence; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the SDS never set up its own party Crisis Staff in Knezevo?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. The SDS never set up its own Crisis Staff. We functioned as state organs, organs of social self-governance throughout the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And the composition was based on your offices, and you acted pursuant to the law which was applied when the Municipal Assembly could not convene.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Municipal Assemblies could not function as bodies of the local commune because of the war. So deputy members of the Assembly were elsewhere and the Secretariats for National Defence took over the duties of Municipal Assemblies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, the executive boards existed, but they were not legislative bodies, which is why they were -- received decisions from the ad hoc bodies, but those decisions had to subsequently be submitted to the Municipal Assembly for approval.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Executive bodies -- boards existed as the executive bodies of those councils, and then the decisions that were issued by the counsel for national defence once the Assemblies could be convened had to be approved by the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness and accused be asked to make pauses between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic and Mr. Komljenovic, you are being asked by the interpreters to put a pause between the question and the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Irrespective of the fact whether those bodies were called War Presidencies or Crisis Staffs or something else, the essence, the composition, and the functioning remained the same irrespective of the name. Did you have commissioners from republican bodies?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that the essence of the work of these organs regardless of whether they were federal Crisis Staffs or War Presidencies, it remained the same both in terms of jurisdiction and also in terms of the persons involved. The persons who were members were usually members ex officio. I didn't understand the second question -- the second part of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you have war commissioners? Remember that the central authorities wanted to have some kind of insight and to be able to send instructions. In your municipality there was no War Commissioner; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have one. We did function properly with a council, with the Executive Board, so civilian authorities fully functioned, and we did not receive any instructions nor did we have any commissioners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, I'm not stopping you asking these lines of questions, but I take it you are fully aware that the municipality of Knezevo or Skender Vakuf is not included -- included in the municipalities of the indictment except for the Koricanske Stijene incident.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Excellency, I fully agree with you. However, this is a rare opportunity for us to see whether there was or was not a pattern, whether the central authorities made municipalities do something. This is an example of a municipality that managed to preserve peace and dignity and was not engulfed in inter-ethnic strife. However, I'm certainly going to bring this to an end.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Had there been a crisis in the functioning of the municipality, although this is a hypothesis, do you think that the government would have sent you a commissioner as well?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we'd probably try to find a solution on our own, and we'd probably turn to the government for that as well. Well, we'd certainly want to receive some kind of support or assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Last question, Mr. Komljenovic. This is what I'd like to ask you: In view of what was going on, are you convinced that we were forced to take certain steps, as one is in chess, forced to make certain moves when the SDA or the HDZ would make us do something? Were we just reacting to the actions that they took? Do you agree with that, because you were a local politician and you knew how the party functioned?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the way it can be put, basically, in view of the official policy of the Serbian Democratic Party. And that is an effort from the point of view of the state and the constitution to preserve what was there, the state as it was, and this effort for Bosnia-Herzegovina to keep its status within Yugoslavia. So it is quite clear that the moves that were made and our responses to that were our referendum, actually, to remain in Yugoslavia. The proclamation of Republika Srpska was actually a response to their violent change of the constitution and of the constitutional legal position of Bosnia-Herzegovina within the state of Yugoslavia. All the problems stemmed from that, all the problems that Bosnia-Herzegovina had, and we as well, all three peoples and the citizens as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd just like to ask you one more thing. You had a convincing majority. The Serbs were a majority in the population, and the party won a majority vote. Did you give Muslims and Croats any positions in government?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The figures were the other way round, not as you put them. Croats 20 per cent and Muslims about 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We strictly took this into account. As far as I know, we had a coalition agreement between the SDA and the HDZ and the SDS about the takeover of power and the establishment of government. The government of Bosnia-Herzegovina was formed in that way, whereas we in the municipality of Knezevo divided portfolios in a similar way in local government. For example, the HDZ got the vice-president of the Executive Board, also the secretary of the Secretariat for National Defence, what we already mentioned, and also the vice-president for Economic Affairs and Social Services. The SDA, well, there were very few of them in Knezevo, rather, Skender. However, we tried to strike a balance in terms of other positions, and we strictly took that into account.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So they did not object in any way; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the contrary. We reached many decisions together. I'm referring to the decisions of the local Assembly. We were very careful not to out-vote the Muslims in any way. We realised that they were not in the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That they were a minority.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A minority, yes. And we did not want anything bad to happen to them in the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Komljenovic. Especially I would like to thank you for having stayed on for so long so that I could spend more than two hours cross-examining you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would also like to thank the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, I have just a couple of matters.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: If we could have Exhibit P3769 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, this is your notebook, and at pages 12 and 13 today, Mr. Karadzic took you to the meeting in Banja Luka on the 30th of August, 1992, and asked you whether certain things were part of the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can just go to those pages, please. And I think it's page 20 of 37 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, you said that those pages that -- the page you see in B/C/S, that's 06397783, was written by Mr. Glamocic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Can we have the correct English page. Thank you. It's the page before that in English, please. Sorry. Page 19.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And then as I understood your -- your -- your testimony, if we go the following page in -- in B/C/S and in English, I understood you to say that the -- the left-hand side of that page written in B/C/S, that's on 06397784, was also part of the meeting and that was the notes that you took.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if we can go to the following page in English as well so that we're on the same pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are my notes. This is my handwriting. However, I said that the right-hand side where it says "president of the court Maric," I'm not sure about that side because I'm not sure that Maric attended the meeting at all. It is possible. Yes, these are my notes, but, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. And that's --

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure. I'm not sure that Maric attended the meeting, but I did write this down. So if that is a whole, as it were, if it's got to do with one particular meeting, then he was there too.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes. But as I understood you, you were unsure whether this -- this other page concerned the meeting and the following page where Mr. Trivic's name is mentioned. Is -- is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I expressed my doubt. I said that it was likely that he did not attend that meeting. It's possible that this was something different, that it's not from that meeting, because I do not remember Trivic being present.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] And under Mr. Maric --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And under Mr. Maric and the check-point there's control of persons who have been mobilised and goods and receiving 100 DM, and again that you -- you were of the view that that wasn't part of the meeting as well; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very, very possible, because I don't see why we would mention 100 Deutschmark at that meeting, or any check-point. It is quite possible that this actually is not from that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I'd now like to -- earlier on at transcript page -- earlier today, you mentioned that -- that just in relation to something that was -- was put in your summary, and you said that you never said in your statement about explosives being put into the abyss. What, in fact, was read out on Thursday at transcript page 20913 as part of the summary was: "The witness stated that there were rumours that the bodies, the remaining bodies, were burnt or explosives were put into the abyss." Do you remember saying that in the Ivankovic trial? And this is at page 34 of the English and page 29 of the B/C/S of 65 ter number 22145, please. And this is, in fact, contained on page 22 of your amalgamated witness statement which is now Exhibit P3768. You were asked by counsel the question: "And was the terrain clearing then finished and did citizens stop coming to you with their complaints about unpleasant odours spreading and similar?" And your -- you answered: "Listen, I am saying again that there were all kinds of rumours, informal and unofficial rumours that they had been heaped over, that they had been mined, that they had been burnt down." Do you recall saying that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. I object to this being part of the redirect examination since it doesn't emanate from the cross, and you told the witness that the summary was not evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think that's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I won't pursue it.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, do you -- do you know that "Glas" is the major newspaper in the Krajina -- Bosnian Krajina area?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And do you --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters's note: We did not hear the witness. Again, we did not hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I heard it but the interpreters --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could you speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- did not hear your answer. Could you kindly repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off because there is a great deal of background noise and we cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, I read it [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: You mentioned at transcript page 19 today that 12 babies died in Banja Luka in July and that nobody did anything about it, humanitarian organisations, nobody.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 23507 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for that if I may intervene in the transcript. The witness said: "I read 'Glas' from time to time." "From time to time" was not recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be looked into.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, do you see this "Glas" article in front of you dated the 4th of June, 1992, the headline is "Breathless Babies"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And talking about Banja Luka, incubated babies lives are endangered. Did you -- do you recall reading this article? Or did you read this article in the "Glas" newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having read it in "Glas," but I know the case of the Banja Luka babies, and I don't know what is in dispute there.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter number 23508.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor does not wish to tender this document, I would like to tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, if Mr. Karadzic wishes to tender it, then he can tender it. But if you -- if -- I'm more than happy to tender it. If -- if -- I was going to tender this one and seek to tender the next one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, let us see.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Do you see, Mr. Komljenovic, 65 ter number 23508 on the screen which is another "Glas" article dated the 8th of June, 1992, headlined "The Oxygen Has Arrived"? Do you recall if -- do you remember reading this article? And it says: "Banja Luka, 5th of June. Three aeroplanes landed at the Banja Luka airport in Mahovljani at about 1300 hours today carrying a cargo of oxygen essential to the activities of health organisations. According to unofficial information, the flight of these aeroplanes was brokered by the International Red Cross and UNPROFOR. 60 bottles of oxygen thus reached Banja Luka." Do you -- do you recall reading this in the "Glas" newspaper?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember having read this. In my view it's not important whether I read it or not. I know that the 12 babies in Banja Luka died, so this probably arrived too late. Late, late.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, do you also read the newspaper "Vreme"?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Vreme" is a Belgrade weekly. Is that what you mean?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seldom, very, very seldom.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would tender those two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Those would be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P3770 and P3771, respectively, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, could I just clarify this part of the redirect that has to do with the diary. It's only going to take two minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let's upload that page.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The D document, I think, that Madam Sutherland had called up.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While we're waiting for this, Mr. Komljenovic, let me ask you this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's Exhibit P3769. Yes, it's coming.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have the previous page, please. The previous page in Serbian. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What is written here, CSB meeting, Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is written there, meeting of the CSB Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Page 13 in e-court in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the previous page it is also the 30th, Banja Luka. Now, let me ask you this: If someone were to mention at that meeting that Maric, president of the court, should be contacted, would you have written that down? Which does not mean that he had to be present there; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Possibly there was some discussion in that context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic put exactly that question to the witness in his cross-examination and the witness already answered it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think so. It won't be necessary for you repeat your question which you put in your cross-examination. Otherwise, then, we'll conclude.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I just wanted to ask whether that would pertain to Trivic or anyone else who could have been mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: That does not necessarily mean that they were present; right?

utterances.speaker: MILAN KOMLJENOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Maric could have been mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Your Honour, that was -- that was already asked and already answered in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you. No further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Komljenovic, that concludes your evidence. I appreciate your coming to The Hague to give it, as well as your indulgence for your agreeing to stay for an extended time. On behalf of my colleagues and the Tribunal, I would like to thank you again, and now you are free to go.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is there anything, Ms. Sutherland?

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Before we take a break for the next witness, there is an issue of scheduling for witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Why don't you raise it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: It's with the witness that's coming after the -- the next witness. Is the -- and I'm inquiring with the Chamber if there 's a possibility to sit an extended session on Wednesday or start earlier, 8.30, on -- on Wednesday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wednesday being --

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Wednesday being tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: And if it's not possible, would it be possible to start either at 8.30 in the morning on Wednesday and Thursday in order to complete that next witness's testimony before 10.00 a.m. on Thursday?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thursday we are supposed to sit from 9.00 to 3.00.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness has a commitment and advised the VWS and/or the OTP of this situation, and he has to leave by 11.00 from the Hague on Thursday. And I note that Your Honours have just given an estimate of three hours for cross-examination, and in order to complete his testimony before 10.00 -- 10.30 at the latest, I think, in order for him to leave The Hague by 11.00 on Thursday, I would ask Your Honours to consider either sitting an extended session on Wednesday or starting half an hour early both on Wednesday and Thursday so that we would complete his testimony before 10.30 a.m. on Thursday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Your plan or suggestion is to interpose the next witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, to -- to follow -- I mean, the witness that I'm speaking of is -- is Edward Vulliamy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. How much time do we need for the next one? You asked for one and a half hours? Originally you asked for just a half hour, but I noted it has been extended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Just the examination-in-chief is expected to consume a little less than an hour for this next witness, Mr. President, if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That's more than the original estimate, which was half an hour. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'd have to check, but I believe that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, with respect to this next witness there's going to be a request for additional time for cross-examination. So it may be better to interpose Mr. Vulliamy in the middle of -- maybe he could start tomorrow morning and interrupt the testimony of the next witness and then we complete Mr. Vulliamy's testimony and we can go back to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How does that suggestion sound to you Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the concern, of course, Mr. President, was the length of time that witness has been here. Preliminary indications are that that will work out, but maybe it's best we confer over the break to make sure in view of the length of time that witness has been here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us do the mathematics during the break and come back to you, but before we bring in the next witness there are a couple of administrative matters that I'd like to deal with in private session. Could the Chamber move into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Unless there are any other matters to raise, then we will take a break for an hour. And let me just consult my court deputy -- yes, Ms. Sutherland.

utterances.speaker: MS. SUTHERLAND
utterances.text: In doing the mathematics over the break, Mr. Robinson said that Mr. Karadzic was going to seek more time for cross-examination of the next witness. I don't know if Mr. Karadzic had -- can indicate approximately how much additional time that he was going to be seeking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't recall how much time we asked for, but we did ask for additional allotments. In any case, at least between four and five hours are necessary for such an important witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: We asked for four hours, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You asked for ten hours for Mr. Komljenovic and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, we're speaking of the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm giving you an example. You asked for ten hours and completed in two and a half, two and 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Actually this was an experiment on my part because I was asked to give this by e-mail instead of putting out our monthly list because it was a delayed disclosure witness. So I decided to give a very realistic estimate and see how the Chamber would react, so I hoped you wouldn't cut it in half or use any formula like that but give something very close to what we asked in that particular case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We will consider that and come back to you after the break. Court deputy, approach the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will resume at quarter past 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.15 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we proceed to hear the evidence of next witness, please be seated for the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There are several administrative matters. First as to the extension of time for Mr. Karadzic's cross-examination of this witness, the -- at the moment, the Chamber sees no reason to extend the time given the factors we considered in reaching the original estimate of the proper amount of cross-examination. And as to the scheduling to accommodate the specific peculiar circumstances regarding the witness after this witness, the Chamber has decided to interpose that witness into the evidence of this witness, i.e., with the indulgence of this witness, we'll proceed to hear the witness next, i.e., Mr. Vulliamy, tomorrow morning. And with the understanding of the staff we are minded to start at 8.30, and with two half-an-hour breaks we will proceed to 2.00, whereby we will get four hours and a half, which in the view of the Chamber is more than sufficient to cover that witness. That said, if the -- we are going to hear this witness's evidence in closed session, so could the Chamber move into closed session now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 9th day of November, 2011, at 8.30 a.m. 23 24 25
